title: One Last Ride

jokes.text: Leslie arrives with comfort food, scrapbooks, and tissues for what is framed as a normal last day at work
jokes.setup: Leslie announces today is the last day they'll all be together and she needs to savor every moment
jokes.punchline: She has brought comfort food, scrapbooks, AND tissues — treating a work farewell like a death
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie over-preparation comedy. The tissues push it from sweet to funny. Strong character integration — only Leslie would treat a farewell with this level of ceremony.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I want our last day together to be absolutely perfect. We'll start with a sunrise hike, then a picnic lunch with those little sandwiches you love, and we'll end the day watching the sunset from that overlook.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And then we'll just sit there in comfortable silence, maybe hold hands, and cry. A lot. Just uncontrollable sobbing. Really ugly crying.

jokes.text: "Good lord." — Ron's deadpan reaction to Leslie's comfort food/scrapbooks/tissues announcement
jokes.setup: Leslie announces she's brought comfort food, scrapbooks, and tissues
jokes.punchline: Ron's entire contempt for sentimentality distilled into two words
jokes.explanation: Peak Ron economy. Two words carry seven seasons of character. The joke IS the character — Ron's stoic horror at Leslie's emotional excess perfectly encapsulated. High character integration score because no other character could make 'Good lord' land this way.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Why don't we just skip to the highlights of our work history?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Skip? Ben, we spent three hours debating whether the coffee machine should go in the break room or the kitchen. That's a highlight.

jokes.text: "Well, today should be perfect. And any perfect day involves crying uncontrollably."
jokes.setup: Leslie declares today should be perfect
jokes.punchline: She sincerely equates a perfect day with uncontrollable crying
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Leslie is NOT being ironic — she genuinely means it. The logical dissonance between 'perfect' and 'crying uncontrollably' is the joke. Strong Leslie characterization; her emotional intensity reframed as joy is a recurring and beloved comic engine.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Johnny Karate says: believe in yourself, and you can accomplish anything!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But realistically, I've tried that and it hasn't worked out great.

jokes.text: Garry's musical number about the pod-based coffee machine that he and Leslie apparently wrote together
jokes.setup: Leslie is going through the comprehensive retrospective and lands on 'The debate about getting a pod-based coffee machine'
jokes.punchline: Garry and Leslie wrote a MUSICAL NUMBER about it — and it is immediately cut off
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of a musical number existing about a coffee machine debate is perfect. The interruption cutting it off before we hear it is the correct comedic choice — the imagination is funnier than execution. Garry's genuine enthusiasm makes it sadder and funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: ♪ Should we get a new coffee machine? (Coffee machine!) / The old one's been here since twenty-thirteen (That's ten years!) / Some say it's broken, some say it's fine / But Jerry's the one who decides in the end, not mine! ♪

jokes.text: "Can't we just quickly shake hands, pretend we liked each other, and get out of here?" — April/Ron trying to escape Leslie's retrospective
jokes.setup: Leslie is launching into a comprehensive retrospective with musical numbers
jokes.punchline: April and Ron propose the bare minimum social contract and bolting
jokes.explanation: Perfect April/Ron alliance joke. The 'pretend we liked each other' is the best part — implying even that is a performance. Character integration is high because only these two would articulate this and mean it sincerely.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: The idea that Gary could ever have dignity

jokes.text: Citizen walks in to report a broken swing mid-Leslie's emotional retrospective
jokes.setup: Leslie is mid-speech about their last day and everything they've shared
jokes.punchline: A random citizen walks in with a mundane parks complaint, completely undercutting the emotional moment
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant. The contrast between the grand emotional moment and the banal citizen complaint is a classic sitcom deflation that also sets up the entire episode's plot. Earned because the show has spent seasons establishing these two registers (civic mundanity vs. Leslie's epic feelings).

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I am going to fix this swing, and I'm going to do it because I want to see Ben's butt.

jokes.text: "'Anything is possible if you follow your dreams.' Johnny Karate. Except getting a swing fixed."
jokes.setup: Citizen asks if they can get a swing fixed; Andy quotes his own children's show character with inspirational wisdom
jokes.punchline: Immediately undercuts it: except getting a swing fixed. None of us work here anymore.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. Three-part structure: inspirational quote, attribution to his own alter ego, immediate self-contradiction. Only Andy Dwyer would quote himself as 'Johnny Karate' as if it's a sage philosopher. The self-deflation is perfectly timed. High quotability because the structure is memorable and the character specificity is total.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ten points to Gryffindor! Wait, no. Ten points to the Parks Department!

jokes.text: "Come on, Garry. You're the mayor now. Have some dignity." — as Garry sings along to the coffee machine musical number
jokes.setup: Garry is enthusiastically singing his own coffee machine musical number
jokes.punchline: Ron chiding him about dignity now that he's mayor — the office of mayor being invoked against a coffee jingle
jokes.explanation: Works on multiple levels: the absurdity of mayoral dignity being invoked for a coffee jingle, Ron's pompous seriousness, and Garry's unironic delight. The snippet of actual lyrics ('Donna said to get rid of me / But Ron was suspicious 'cause my coffee was delicious') makes this even richer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: It's called 'A lot of Forms to Love,' like the Beatles song 'A Lot of Love to Love'... wait, no. 'All You Need is Love.' I combined 'forms' with 'for.' Get it?

jokes.text: Coffee machine musical number lyrics revealed: 'The vote was four to three / Donna said to get rid of me / But Ron was suspicious 'cause my coffee was delicious'
jokes.setup: The existence of a musical number about a coffee machine debate
jokes.punchline: The actual lyrics are revealed — they're earnest, rhymey, and treat the coffee debate like a genuine drama with real stakes
jokes.explanation: The lyrics are genuinely funny on their own — the internal rhyme, the dramatic narrative arc of a coffee machine vote, the specific detail of Ron being suspicious because the coffee was delicious. Earned and absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I heard you got kicked out of En Vogue.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I kicked them out. I was too fabulous.

jokes.text: Ben reveals he preemptively booked a backup flight because he 'figured something like this would happen'
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Ben to cancel the 11am flight because they have work here
jokes.punchline: Ben already booked a 6pm backup because he knows Leslie so completely
jokes.explanation: A warm, character-specific joke. Ben's competence as Leslie's partner — knowing she will derail any plan — is both funny and endearing. The relationship dynamic carries the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: They're building something called 'Space Haystack' around the Space Needle.

jokes.text: "I love you. You're perfect. You get me. I'm so glad I am married to you. I cannot wait to fix that swing so we can get your little butt right into it."
jokes.setup: Leslie is touched that Ben booked a backup flight and begins a heartfelt declaration of love
jokes.punchline: The romantic sentiment peaks and then pivots to 'I cannot wait to fix that swing so we can get your little butt right into it' — her motivation for romance being a civic project
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation structure. The love declaration follows a perfect comedic arc into the absurd kicker. 'I cannot wait to fix that swing so we can get your little butt right into it' is a perfectly weird line — ambiguous, then clarified. The 'I know it's weird. Whatever. It motivates me.' self-awareness pushes it further.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: I can barely see the Space Needle.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: That's intentional.

jokes.text: "Correct. Five points for Hufflepuff."
jokes.setup: Someone correctly names the parks requisition form
jokes.punchline: Leslie awards Hufflepuff points as if they're in Harry Potter — a completely unearned reference
jokes.explanation: Solidly funny, very Leslie — the way she immediately defaults to a rewards system even in an unstructured moment. The Hufflepuff specificity (not Gryffindor, which would be the expected choice for a 'hero') adds a small wrinkle. Slightly cheap pop culture reference but character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Coffee and marijuana. That's why the Seattle real estate market moves so fast. People are either wired or high, and they're making major life decisions.

jokes.text: Leslie kept a physical requisition form in her scrapbook titled 'Thanks Form the Memories!'
jokes.setup: Everyone points out they can't file the form because the system is digital and they have no logins
jokes.punchline: Leslie produces a physical form from a scrapbook — which is titled 'Thanks Form the Memories!' (a pun on 'Thanks FOR the Memories')
jokes.explanation: Two-layer joke: (1) Leslie's scrapbook compulsion saving the day, which is character-perfect, and (2) the pun in the scrapbook title ('Form' instead of 'For') — a pun that only Leslie would make about a government form. The word 'Form' being the pun is a lovely nerdy Parks detail.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: They cut the math club.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? That's terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: Yeah, it gets worse. They've cut math entirely.

jokes.text: Donna's story about getting kicked out of En Vogue — 'Technically, I kicked them out.'
jokes.setup: Leslie references 'that crazy story about you getting kicked out of En Vogue'
jokes.punchline: Donna corrects the framing with total composure: 'Technically, I kicked them out.'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and character integration. The correction is delivered with zero drama, which is everything. It raises more questions than it answers (how does one kick out En Vogue?), and Donna's absolute confidence in this framing is the joke. One of the episode's most quotable moments. The 'technically' is doing enormous comedic work.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Hi, is this Satan? It's your son.

jokes.text: "I'm married to a teacher, and I love the man, but I also love diamond watches."
jokes.setup: Donna explains she needs her real estate license because she's moving to Seattle
jokes.punchline: The frank acknowledgment that love of husband and love of luxury are parallel and coequal motivations
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Donna. The comma separating love of Joe from love of diamond watches is the whole joke — they are syntactically equal. No guilt, no apology. Character integration is near-perfect; this line could only be Donna.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm going to treat yo' self with Joe.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: Wait, what? I'm not on the menu.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: We're going shopping and getting massages.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: Oh. That's... that's nice.

jokes.text: The 'Space Haystack' being built around the Space Needle until you can barely see the needle anymore — 'I know. It's kind of the point.'
jokes.setup: Donna describes their potential Seattle house — 3,400 sq ft with a view of Puget Sound
jokes.punchline: The window looks out on the 'new Space Haystack' being built around the Space Needle — the needle is almost invisible. 'I know. It's kind of the point.'
jokes.explanation: A fun background absurdist gag — the Space Haystack is a genuinely original invention and the deadpan explanation ('it's kind of the point') makes it funnier. Lower character integration because this could be any character's future city.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I started the hoop earring trend in the '90s. Nobody was wearing them, and then I wore them, and now everybody wears them. That was me.

jokes.text: "I think it's all that coffee and legal marijuana. Has people wanting to buy houses quickly and irrationally."
jokes.setup: The Seattle house sold in two hours
jokes.punchline: Donna's theory: coffee + legal weed = irrational rapid home purchases
jokes.explanation: Competent observational humor about Seattle culture. Gets a solid chuckle. Nothing exceptional but the delivery would be smooth.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I'm very zen. I meditate every morning. My mantra is: 'Craig is a virtue. Craig is a virtue. Craig is a virtue.'

jokes.text: "Middle Korea was so beautiful."
jokes.setup: Donna says this year's Donna-Joe adventure quest can't beat last year's
jokes.punchline: Last year they went to 'Middle Korea' — a place that does not exist — treated as totally normal
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and originality. Two words — 'Middle Korea' — create an entire absurdist geography, delivered with zero explanation or fanfare. The show never clarifies what Middle Korea is, which is the correct choice. One of the best background jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: When Craig first moved in, I thought he was just a little quirky. Then I thought maybe he was a serial killer. Then I thought, you know what, I should probably call the police.

jokes.text: "Call Satan's niece." — Donna's contact name for April
jokes.setup: Donna pulls out her phone to call April
jokes.punchline: The audience sees April's contact name in Donna's phone is 'Satan's niece'
jokes.explanation: Perfect character-to-character joke. 'Satan's niece' rather than 'Satan' herself is the key detail — it implies a family relationship to evil but with the slightly diminished status of a niece. Could only be April's contact name. High character integration for both Donna (blunt labeling) and April (dark persona).

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I'm Craig Middlebrooks, the Parks Department's Multiplayer Rec Coordinator. I'm also an accomplished singer. I have the voice of an angel trapped in the body of a man who has seen some things.

jokes.text: Andy showing Donna a photo of himself DJing a boat party in Venezuela — "Kind of reminded me of the two weeks you and I spent there. Oh, yeah. That happened."
jokes.setup: Andy approaches Donna with photos on his phone
jokes.punchline: Andy and Donna apparently spent two weeks in Venezuela together, which is news to the audience — Donna's 'Yeah, it did' followed immediately by 'April!' suggests she's eager to change the subject
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the unexplained shared history between the two most unlikely characters, delivered as if it requires no elaboration. 'Oh yeah. That happened.' from Donna — acknowledging without unpacking — is a great deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: You know what? I lied. I have thousands of regrets. Including this meal we're eating right now.

jokes.text: "Are you gonna buy me a bunch of leather handbags?" — April's assumption of what 'Treat Yo' Self' means
jokes.setup: Andy announces he's decided to 'treat yo self' April
jokes.punchline: April, whose aesthetic is gothic and contrary, immediately assumes leather handbags as the treat — showing a hidden materialism
jokes.explanation: A small character reveal — April's cynicism about gifts pivoting to surprisingly materialistic hope. The leather specificity is right for April. Decent but not standout.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Shotgun!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're just taking the elevator to the fourth floor.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know. Shotgun means I get to push the button.

jokes.text: The 'Teach Yo' Self' foundation — Donna redirecting 'Treat Yo' Self' money to an education charity
jokes.setup: Andy built up the 'Treat Yo' Self' reveal; April expects luxury gifts
jokes.punchline: The actual treat is an education charity called 'Teach Yo' Self' — a pun on the running gag phrase, but earnest
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback that subverts the original 'Treat Yo' Self' concept into something generous. The wordplay is clean and the emotional turn is earned. Works as both a joke and a character moment for Donna's growth.

dialogue.speaker: Ethel Beavers
dialogue.line: You're a Luddite!

jokes.text: Donna's list of personal adventures: 'I single-handedly started that door-knockers earring trend. I came in ninth in Italy's Got Talent. I served on a NASCAR pit crew.'
jokes.setup: Donna explains she's had a lot of adventures and wants a new kind
jokes.punchline: The list of adventures escalates from plausible (earring trend) to surprising (Italy's Got Talent, ninth place!) to absurd (NASCAR pit crew)
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Three-item list with perfect escalation: the specificity of 'ninth' in Italy's Got Talent (not first, not last — ninth) is the funniest detail, implying a genuine compete. The NASCAR pit crew is a total non-sequitur from her persona. High quotability because the list structure is memorable and each item is independently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Agent Macklin here. We've got a situation. A sapphire with the power to restart a historical event. We're talking about a gemstone that could change everything. The president doesn't know about it. Congress doesn't know about it. Only three people in the world know about it, and two of them are dead.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So we're down to me. And this sapphire. And apparently, it can restart the Civil War.

jokes.text: "I am calm. I am grateful. I am Craig." — Craig's entrance mantra
jokes.setup: The team is in Craig's office unexpectedly; Craig enters doing a personal affirmation
jokes.punchline: 'I am Craig' as the third affirmation — treating his own name as a calming identity anchor
jokes.explanation: Fantastic in its simplicity. The escalation from 'I am calm' (normal) to 'I am grateful' (still normal) to 'I am Craig' (his own name as existential anchor) is perfect. It implies Craig has had to remind himself who he is as a grounding technique. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We should make love during the roleplay.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Is this real? Are we actually doing this right now?

jokes.text: Leslie's progressive re-evaluation of Craig: 'There is a man who loves his job... Oh, wow. He's intense... Oh, no. He's insane... That person is psychotic, and I need to call the police.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Craig how she felt when she first met him
jokes.punchline: Her four-stage journey from impressed to terrified, ending with wanting to call the police
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation structure — four distinct stages each landing harder. The final beat ('I need to call the police') is the correct comedic endpoint. Craig's 'Yeah. That's usually the way it goes.' response is the perfect button — his total acceptance of being perceived this way.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Did you eat all the Halloween candy?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No! Well, yes. But that's not the point.

jokes.text: Craig's confessional: 'My name is Craig Middlebrooks. I'm the part-time sommelier here at Tom's Bistro. And I'm a very good singer!'
jokes.setup: Craig's talking head — seemingly about his job at Tom's Bistro
jokes.punchline: The non-sequitur pivot to 'And I'm a very good singer!' delivered with absolute conviction
jokes.explanation: The non-sequitur works because it's delivered with the same gravity as the professional information. Craig's need to establish his singing credentials in a bio-statement is very him.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey babe, I wanted to talk to you about maybe having a babe soon.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Did you just call me babe and then say babe?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I did. Is that weird?

jokes.text: A bar patron sends Craig a glass of wine and his business card — Craig's love story begins
jokes.setup: Craig's confessional establishes him as a part-time sommelier and good singer
jokes.punchline: A bar patron sends him wine and a business card — the absurdly romantic meet-cute for the previously unhinged Craig
jokes.explanation: The comedy is mostly structural — that the most intense, allegedly unhinged character gets the most classically romantic meet-cute. The audience's knowledge of Craig makes the sweetness funny.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I want a little April.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A little version of you. A tiny April.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's the creepiest thing you've ever said.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, what if we had a boy? We could call him Boy April.

jokes.text: Craig's wedding: 'I don't know about this. I'm very scared.' / 'Oh, just relax, you nervous Nellie. You're right. We love each other. And the tax break is substantial.'
jokes.setup: Craig expresses wedding-day nerves
jokes.punchline: Typhoon's reassurance escalates from 'we love each other' (sweet) to 'the tax break is substantial' (mercenary) with equal weight
jokes.explanation: The pivot to 'the tax break is substantial' as an equally valid marriage motivation is the joke. The structure is tight — love is the setup, tax is the punchline. Works well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm a sexy cowgirl astronaut! It's a mashup of two iconic American archetypes.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What are you supposed to be?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I don't get it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Cowgirl. Astronaut. It's not that complicated.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, I mean what's the reference?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Is it from something?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's from... imagination. And America.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So it's not from anything.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Fine. I'm just a girl in a weird outfit.

jokes.text: Craig and Typhoon's anniversary: 'Do you have any regrets? Not one. Not a single one.' / 'Do you have any regrets? Are you kidding? Thousands! Most recently, this trout!'
jokes.setup: An anniversary dinner — Craig asks if Typhoon has regrets, Typhoon asks Craig the same
jokes.punchline: The asymmetric responses: Craig: none. Typhoon: thousands, and he is currently having one about a trout
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect mirror-comedy — identical question, opposite answers. But the kicker 'Most recently, this trout!' is what elevates it to exceptional. The specificity of the trout (a bad fish dish AT THIS ANNIVERSARY DINNER) is simultaneously a relationship comedy, a food joke, and a character revelation. High quotability because 'Most recently, this trout!' is genuinely memorable and transferable.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm going as Kerplunk. You know, the game where you pull out sticks and try not to let the marbles fall?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I looked up reviews online and one of them said it was 'punishingly intricate.'

jokes.text: "One last journey to the weirdest place on earth? Yes." / "Shotgun! W-we're just taking the elevator." / "I get to push the buttons! I called it!"
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if anyone wants to go to the fourth floor to file the form
jokes.punchline: Andy calls shotgun on an elevator, then argues his right to push the buttons
jokes.explanation: Andy calling shotgun on an elevator is a perfect Andy joke — the childlike logic applied to adult situations. Leslie and Ron's reactions carry the moment. 'Oh. He called it.' from Ron is the deadpan button.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You want to play Cones of Dunshire?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, I was lying.

jokes.text: Ethel Beavers tells them the office has gone digital: 'Get with the times, you Luddite.'
jokes.setup: The team presents a physical form to Ethel to be filed
jokes.punchline: The ancient Ethel Beavers (a recurring running gag character) tells THEM to get with the times
jokes.explanation: The reversal — the notoriously old-guard Ethel calling someone else a Luddite — is the joke. Works well because it also advances the plot (can't file the form) while getting a laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: There's nothing more beautiful than children laughing and playing together. It just fills me with hope for the future.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I was so moved by it that I started crying. Those kids were having the time of their lives.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Turns out they were laughing at me falling off the jungle gym.

jokes.text: Andy's Pawnee food farewell: 'I'm gonna miss the food in Pawnee — Taco Bell-KFC, Pizza Hut.'
jokes.setup: Andy is listing what he'll miss about Pawnee
jokes.punchline: The food he'll miss is entirely fast food chains — not local cuisine, not Leslie's cooking
jokes.explanation: Classic Andy simplicity. 'Taco Bell-KFC' being a real Pawnee institution (a long-running Parks gag) adds to it. The juxtaposition with his heartfelt 'And most of all, I'm gonna miss you, Leslie' makes the food list funnier in retrospect.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm worried we might not be able to have kids.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, if it helps, I have three. I could give you one.

jokes.text: April and Andy's Janet Snakehole / Burt Macklin Halloween roleplay — 'Damn it, Macklin! I love it when you take charge! I must have you. I know it's against protocol, but make love to me, you fool! You animal!'
jokes.setup: April is in character as Janet Snakehole; Andy is Burt Macklin handling a sapphire heist
jokes.punchline: The roleplay escalates rapidly into Janet demanding Burt make love to her while children are about to arrive for trick-or-treat
jokes.explanation: A beloved callback to the Snakehole/Macklin running gag, elevated by the timing (trick-or-treaters about to arrive) and Andy's genuine willingness to immediately act on it: 'Wait. Seriously? I -- 'cause I will go do that right now.' Perfect character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ben and Leslie only had sex once. That's how they got three kids.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No, that's not how—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah. One time. Super efficient.

jokes.text: Trick-or-treaters interrupt the Snakehole/Macklin roleplay — Andy realizes they ate all the candy
jokes.setup: April says 'They're here' urgently; Andy and April prepare for something dramatic
jokes.punchline: It's just trick-or-treaters, and also, Andy ate all the candy
jokes.explanation: The double deflation (spy thriller tension → kids at the door → no candy) works efficiently. Andy eating all the candy is entirely predictable but earned.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Kids are the opposite of their parents. So if we're cool, our kids are going to be lame.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Which is great, because then we won't have to worry about them stealing our friends.

jokes.text: Andy's case for having children: 'Yes, I would love all the awesome stuff my body would go through. I mean, if all it meant was puking and getting weird stretch marks and veins everywhere, then sign me up. But at the end, we've brought a child into the world. That's disgusting.'
jokes.setup: Andy wants kids; April is resistant. Andy makes his case for having children.
jokes.punchline: Andy's argument includes enthusiastically endorsing pregnancy symptoms as positives, then concluding 'That's disgusting' about the baby — reversing the expected emotional beat
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. Andy WANTS kids but his argument for having them inadvertently includes endorsing gross pregnancy symptoms AND calling the baby 'disgusting.' The reversal works because Andy is genuinely enthusiastic about the wrong things. 'They wipe all of the disgusting stuff off of it immediately' as a rebuttal to April is perfect. Only Andy Dwyer argues for children this way.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know, April, having children is like expanding your team. You start with just yourself, maybe a partner, and then you add new members who bring fresh perspectives and energy to the group.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So you're saying I should treat my potential kids like employees?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Exactly! And just like any good manager, you want to make sure you're ready before you expand. You need the right resources, the right support system, and a five-year plan.

jokes.text: "I want a little April... Or even a little... Boy April."
jokes.setup: Andy describes wanting children
jokes.punchline: His vision of a son is just 'boy April' — he doesn't conceive of a son as a different type of person from his wife
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The pause before 'Boy April' — as if he's retrieving the concept — is perfect comedic timing on the page. The idea that Andy's ideal son is just a male version of his wife reveals how completely April is his world. Deeply character-specific, economical, and genuinely touching AND funny simultaneously. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We should pick a Halloween-themed baby name!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: How about Omen? Or Pestilence? Or we could name him Divorce, so it'll be easier when he leaves us.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, no.

jokes.text: 'No. They wipe all of the disgusting stuff off of it immediately.' — Andy defending newborns
jokes.setup: April says 'we've brought a child into the world — that's disgusting'
jokes.punchline: Andy reassures her that the disgusting stuff is removed immediately — addressing her concern with complete literal-mindedness
jokes.explanation: Andy takes April's objection entirely at face value and addresses it practically. The sweetness of his literal-mindedness is funny — he genuinely thinks 'but they wipe it off!' is a persuasive argument. Classic Andy earnestness.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so I want to incorporate all my personas into the baby name. We got Burt Macklin, FBI agent. We got Travesty, the coyote. We got Johnny Karate, the martial arts guy. So I'm thinking we call him Burt Travesty Macklin Karate Agent Coyote.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're calling him Jack.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Jack works.

jokes.text: Ben's costume: 'I am the Lamplighter, a character from my new board-game sequel "Cones of Dunshire: Winds of Tremorrah." Gameplay Magazine called it "punishingly intricate."'
jokes.setup: Halloween party; everyone shows off their costumes
jokes.punchline: Ben is dressed as a character from his own board game sequel — and proudly cites 'punishingly intricate' as if it's a positive review
jokes.explanation: Perfect Ben comedy. Dressing as a character from his own board game is the right level of nerd. But 'punishingly intricate' being the chosen quote from Gameplay Magazine — and Ben saying it with clear pride — is the joke. He has selected the most off-putting review as his advertisement.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I have a very particular set of skills. Skills I've acquired over a very long career. Skills that make me a nightmare for people like you. If you change that birth certificate now, that'll be the end of it. I will not look for you, I will not pursue you. But if you don't, I will look for you, I will find you, and I will make you change it.

jokes.text: Leslie's costume: 'I am Sandra Dee... O'Connor. Get it? Sandra Dee plus Sandra Day O'Connor?' / 'Who's Sandra Dee?' / 'Who's Sandra Day O'Connor?'
jokes.setup: Leslie reveals her costume with evident pride in the mashup concept
jokes.punchline: Neither reference lands — April doesn't know the pop star, Andy doesn't know the Supreme Court Justice — making the mashup doubly inaccessible
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant. Leslie's costume is a clever pun — but the joke is that both references are dead to her audience. April's ignorance of Sandra Dee and Andy's ignorance of Sandra Day O'Connor are perfectly character-appropriate failures, and together they make the costume 100% ineffective. Leslie's 'Forget it.' sells the defeat. One of the episode's strongest jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Welcome to the team, little guy! You're going to do great things. I can already tell you're a go-getter. Look at you, already here, already existing. That's the kind of initiative I love to see.

jokes.text: "All right. Let's play." / '...No.' — April pretending to agree to Cones of Dunshire
jokes.setup: Ben promises April would love Cones of Dunshire if she just played once
jokes.punchline: April agrees ('All right. Let's play.') — Ben lights up — then immediately: 'No.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat joke. Maximum economy — four words total for setup ('All right. Let's play.') and one for punchline ('No.'). The pause between them is everything. Entirely character-specific to April. Ben's implicit crushed reaction makes it land harder. One of the episode's most efficient jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Leslie, I need a final favor. Can you help me commit insurance fraud?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jean-Ralphio, no! I can't help you with that.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Okay, okay. How about you fall in love with me instead?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not happening either.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Fine. Will you at least let me smell your socks?

jokes.text: Ben lures Andy to the kitchen 'to give him a hand' — Andy is impressed by this as 'secret agent stuff'
jokes.setup: Ben asks Andy to give him a hand in the kitchen; Andy asks what he needs
jokes.punchline: Ben's 'I just thought you might want to talk' — the kitchen ruse — impresses Andy as a slick secret agent move
jokes.explanation: Andy's genuine admiration of the most mundane social maneuvering is good character comedy. 'That's some secret-agent stuff right there' about a perfectly ordinary conversational redirect is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: It's not weird.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Okay, it's a fetish.

jokes.text: Andy's story about crying at children playing: 'I almost started crying. Granted, I'd just face-planted on my rollerblades. That's what they were laughing at.'
jokes.setup: Andy describes an emotional moment watching children play at the park — building toward a touching moment about wanting kids
jokes.punchline: The kids were laughing at Andy after he face-planted on his rollerblades — not a pure moment of childhood joy
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection executed perfectly. Andy builds what sounds like a genuinely touching reason to want kids, then the reveal recontextualizes the entire scene. 'That's what they were laughing at. Sure. It was emotional.' — Ben's 'Sure.' is the perfect deadpan button. High character integration: only Andy would have this exact experience and still draw the same emotional conclusion.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: We're not suspicious! We're not suspicious!

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: We're not suspicious! We're not suspicious!

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Nothing to see here, we're just two normal people leaving the hospital in the middle of the night!

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: We're not suspicious! We're not suspicious!

jokes.text: "Take one of our kids. We don't need all three."
jokes.setup: Andy asks 'What if she doesn't?' (come around to wanting kids)
jokes.punchline: Ben casually offers to give Andy one of his three children — then immediately clarifies he's kidding
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark-subversive joke from the normally earnest Ben. 'We don't need all three' is the key phrase — the breezy surplus-children framing. Andy's 'Oh my God, Ben. Thank you.' accepting it genuinely makes it better. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Leslie, I got you a parting gift. You know who you remind me of? Yoko Ono. Not because of the music or the art, but because of your body.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's disgusting.

jokes.text: April's rant to Leslie about kids: 'You guys got so lucky. You had sex one time, and you had three kids, and they're all, like, smart and great and healthy.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is about to give April a pep talk about kids
jokes.punchline: April preemptively riffs on how unfairly perfect Ben and Leslie's life is, including the 'you had sex one time' accusation
jokes.explanation: April's rant is genuinely funny because it's simultaneously self-pitying and kind of accurate as a character read of Ben and Leslie. 'You had sex one time' is the quotable line — absurd but delivered with total conviction.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Hey Tom, can you please stop calling me 'accounting nerd'? Just use my name.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Absolutely not. That's your name now. You're the accounting nerd. Deal with it, accounting nerd.

jokes.text: "You think that's the only time we had sex?" / "Yes!"
jokes.setup: April claims Ben and Leslie had sex only once and got three kids
jokes.punchline: Leslie challenges this; April's 'Yes!' confirms it as her genuine belief
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-line exchange. The 'Yes!' is the punchline — April's complete sincerity in this belief about Ben and Leslie. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You should add calzones to the menu.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Calzones are just pizza that's afraid of its own flavor.

jokes.text: April's theory: 'Kids act the opposite of their parents, so that's why your kids are so cool. But Andy and I are cool already, so our kids will be, like, really lame and weird.'
jokes.setup: April is listing reasons not to have kids
jokes.punchline: April's pop-genetics theory concludes she and Andy are too cool to have good kids — their coolness would invert into lameness
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The internal logic is absurd but perfectly consistent. April's framework — cool parents = lame kids, therefore her coolness is a liability — is delivered with total conviction. It's also a sincere expression of her fear disguised as ironic posturing, which makes it emotionally resonant as well as funny.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: Tom Haverford's business ventures had a troubling pattern of failure. But perhaps the most devastating blow came when he was forced to admit he had become... swaggerless.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: In Tom's mind, poverty was survivable. But a life without swagger? That was truly rock bottom.

jokes.text: April giving birth in full Halloween makeup — 'Can I get a warm towel to get that makeup off?' / 'No! I want it on! That's the whole point. I put the makeup on after I went into labor.'
jokes.setup: April is in labor; a doctor asks if they can remove her Halloween makeup
jokes.punchline: April refuses — she put the makeup on AFTER going into labor, because delivering on Halloween was too important to miss
jokes.explanation: A perfect April moment. The detail that she applied the makeup AFTER going into labor — meaning she prioritized Halloween aesthetics mid-contraction — is exactly who April is. High character integration. The visual of a woman giving birth in full Halloween makeup is inherently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.line: The completely unpredictable national beef shortage

jokes.text: Andy's birth mix playing 'Monster Mash' during labor contractions
jokes.setup: April is about to push; Andy insists on playing his 'birth mix'
jokes.punchline: The birth mix is 'Monster Mash' — and it plays through contractions as the doctor coaches April
jokes.explanation: Andy's birth mix being Monster Mash is character-perfect. The interweaving of 'He did the mash / He did the monster mash' with 'Here comes a contraction. Are you ready?' is a great structural joke — the mundanity of medical coaching against the absurdity of Monster Mash. Very Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I just watched the greatest movie ever made. It's called 'Butt: The Movie.'

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: How much did it make at the box office?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: 847 million dollars.

jokes.text: April goes into labor on Halloween and insists on keeping the monster makeup on during delivery
jokes.setup: April is going into labor
jokes.punchline: 'I want it on! That's the whole point. I put the makeup on after I went into labor.' — April went into labor and THEN applied monster makeup for the occasion
jokes.explanation: The detail that April applied the monster makeup AFTER going into labor is exceptional. It implies she stopped at some point during labor onset to carefully put on face paint — this is both very funny and deeply in character. The reveal 'I put the makeup on after I went into labor' has great comic timing. The doctor's 'whatever blows your skirt up' is a perfect understated response.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The movie's called 'Danger: Maximum.'

jokes.text: Naming the baby: 'Burt Macklin Jr.?' / 'We need a Halloween angle. How about Demon Spawn Baby Satan Dwyer?' / 'Or, uh... Maybe Burt Snakehole Ludgate Karate Dracula Macklin Demon Jack-o'-Lantern Dwyer? We call him Jack for short?'
jokes.setup: The baby is born; they need to name him
jokes.punchline: The name escalates to 'Burt Snakehole Ludgate Karate Dracula Macklin Demon Jack-o'-Lantern Dwyer' with 'Jack for short' — collapsing a 10-word name into four letters
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The full name is a perfect synthesis of every running character both Andy and April have embodied, plus Halloween elements. The escalation structure is flawless. 'We call him Jack for short' lands the punchline beautifully — the absurd compression from 10 words to one. A callback that rewards loyal viewers while being funny on its own terms.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What should you not be?

dialogue.speaker: Audience
dialogue.line: Don't be Gary! Don't be Gary! Don't be Gary!

jokes.text: Andy trying to bribe/Liam-Neeson the doctor into changing the birth certificate to show Halloween instead of November 1st
jokes.setup: The baby was born at 12:06 a.m. on November 1st; Andy wants it changed to 11:59 p.m. on Halloween
jokes.punchline: Andy's escalation: first offering a Yelp review, then delivering the 'Taken' monologue at the doctor
jokes.explanation: The Taken monologue from Andy Dwyer — a man trying to get a Halloween birthday for his child — is a perfect absurdist escalation. 'I'll give you a good review on Yelp' as the first negotiating tactic is itself funny. The doctor's 'Is that the monologue from Taken?' followed by Andy's complete success ('My son was born on Halloween. Do you understand? Yes, I do. That's awesome. Thank you.') is a wonderful joke about the power of movie speeches.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I wrote you a little message in the front of this book. It says, 'To Leslie, may your life be as filled with wonder and enchantment as the pages of this book.' You know what that means?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, what?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Absolutely nothing. I have no idea what I'm talking about. I just wanted to give you a book.

jokes.text: Andy delivers the 'Taken' monologue to a doctor to get a birth certificate changed, verbatim
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to convince a doctor to change the birth certificate date
jokes.punchline: He deploys the iconic Taken speech ('I have a particular set of skills...') as actual intimidation, delivered with complete commitment
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the gap between the gravitas of the Taken speech and the stakes of the request (a birth certificate date change). The doctor's clarification 'Is that the monologue from Taken?' followed by Andy's unashamed 'My son was born on Halloween. Do you understand?' and the doctor caving is a well-paced exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Brandi Maxxx
dialogue.line: Yeah, I've been really busy with my film production company. Last month alone I completed 847 movies.

jokes.text: Garry's delivery journey with Leslie: 'It seems only right that we make this journey one final time.' — Leslie clearly imagines a sentimental walk; it is to the maintenance room
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Garry to accompany her for one final time, framing it sentimentally
jokes.punchline: The destination is the maintenance room — and the 'great conversations and bonding moments' Leslie describes were about delivering a form
jokes.explanation: Decent Leslie-Garry dynamic joke. Leslie's capacity to imbue any mundane task with grandeur is a solid character note. Functional but not standout.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Even at Gary's funeral, Gayle's wearing that outfit.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What's wrong with it?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Nothing, it's just... she looks amazing. Gary's in a casket and she looks like she's going to brunch in the Hamptons.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio appearing in a hospital bed: 'You're not injured?' / 'Uh, yeah. I'm injured. I got a terminal case of "Get me to the front of the line at Six Flags."'
jokes.setup: Tom and Leslie visit Jean-Ralphio in a hospital bed, concerned
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio has faked a terminal illness to get Six Flags front-of-line access
jokes.explanation: Excellent Jean-Ralphio joke. The term 'terminal case of Get me to the front of the line at Six Flags' is a wonderfully specific scam. The medical framing applied to transparent grift is perfect for the character. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Well, that's fitting. Gary's name has been misspelled on pretty much every document in this town for the last thirty years. At least they got the dates right.

jokes.text: "It's a winter wonderland!" — Jean-Ralphio gesturing at his fake hospital setup
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is showing off his fake hospital scam
jokes.punchline: He describes his elaborate fake-injury setup as 'a winter wonderland' — inexplicably and enthusiastically
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's chaotic energy distilled into a completely non-sequitur exclamation. Works because of the character, not the writing.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: I was talking to this guy online for three weeks. We had so much in common. Turns out he was catfishing me. But here's the thing – he wasn't pretending to be someone more attractive. He was pretending to be someone who liked the same obscure 90s folk music as me. That's what got me. Not the fake photos of him skydiving or whatever. It was the carefully curated Spotify playlist of Neutral Milk Hotel deep cuts.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio's final request: 'Will you pretend to be my wife for an insurance scam? But then we fall in love for real! Also, can I have a pair of your gym socks? No, wait. It's not for anything weird. It's just a fetish I have.'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio asks Leslie for one final kindness
jokes.punchline: The request escalates: insurance scam → romantic love subplot → gym sock fetish, self-described as 'not weird'
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jean-Ralphio escalation. Three layers of increasingly inappropriate requests, each delivered with the same breezy confidence. 'It's not for anything weird. It's just a fetish I have.' — the self-correction that confirms the weirdness is the joke. Extremely character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: He texted me from the altar. He said, 'I can't do this. I'm in the middle of a raid.'

jokes.text: Leslie's farewell to Jean-Ralphio: 'Although I truly hope that I never see you again, I do wish you a long and happy life.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is saying goodbye to Jean-Ralphio
jokes.punchline: The farewell is structured as a compliment but leads with 'I truly hope I never see you again' — anti-sentiment as sentiment
jokes.explanation: Very well constructed. Leslie's warmth and Jean-Ralphio's exhausting chaos collide in this line. She sincerely means both parts — she does wish him happiness AND she hopes never to deal with him again. The honesty makes it funnier than a standard insult. High quotability and transferable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've repaired this swing. That'll be $6.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio's fake funeral — 'Bend Over' by Lil Jon featuring Tyga as his favorite song played at the service
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio's 'funeral' — he has faked his death as an insurance scam
jokes.punchline: His 'favorite song' per his last will and testament is 'Bend Over' by Lil Jon featuring Tyga, which plays at the solemn service
jokes.explanation: The solemnity of 'as per his last will and testament' introducing 'Bend Over' by Lil Jon is a perfect setup/punchline. The song choice is maximally inappropriate for a funeral but maximally appropriate for Jean-Ralphio. The fact that it's actually playing — and we hear 'Bend over, make your knees touch your elbows' — makes it better.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't know what you want me to do here. Crying? Public displays of emotion? It's not gonna happen. I'm leaving because I found a better opportunity, not because I'm going to sit around and feel feelings about it.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio and Mona-Lisa reveal the scam: 'They bought it. They bought it. Do you have the insurance money?' / 'No doubt, no doubt. Let's hit it, bro. Time to start a casino in... Tajikistan!'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio faked his death for an insurance scam
jokes.punchline: The insurance money is destined for... a casino in Tajikistan. Which he sings about.
jokes.explanation: Tajikistan as the casino destination is a wonderfully specific absurdist choice. Jean-Ralphio singing 'Tajikistan / A-a-a-n / Tajikistan' to a self-composed jingle while Mona-Lisa joins in is peak Saperstein energy. 'This is the best idea you've ever had.' / 'No, no, no. This is God's idea. I'm just the vessel.' is also a great beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So Ron, if you invest in this emerging spirits portfolio, you could see significant returns in 3-5 years.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Ben, are you telling me I could own a whiskey company?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, not own it outright, but you'd have a substantial stake in several premium distilleries.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Which distilleries?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Including Lagavulin.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm listening.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio, caught mid-escape: 'God! Tajikistan is off! Go, go, go, go! The rabbi!'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is caught by someone at the fake funeral
jokes.punchline: The Tajikistan casino plan is immediately abandoned at the sight of the rabbi; 'The rabbi!' as the specific doom signal
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'Tajikistan is off' works as a button to the fake funeral sequence. The rabbi as the undoing of the plan raises interesting unexplored questions that add to the absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Ben is a good friend. We have a professional relationship based on mutual respect and a shared commitment to our work.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio's parting declaration to Tom: 'Leslie... I've always loved you.' / 'I know.'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio says something seemingly heartfelt while fleeing
jokes.punchline: He directs 'I've always loved you' to Leslie (not Tom, his best friend), and Leslie's 'I know' is a perfectly dry acceptance
jokes.explanation: Small but very funny — Jean-Ralphio directing his love confession at Leslie rather than Tom while fleeing, and Leslie's calm 'I know' suggesting she's always known and it's fine. Perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jen Barkley
dialogue.line: Sorry to interrupt, but we need to talk about the campaign. Now. Everyone else needs to leave.

jokes.text: Jamm's parting gift: a photo of him and Leslie's face Photoshopped onto Yoko Ono's body — 'Horrifying.' / 'Yeah, Yoko had a real killer bod. Just like you.'
jokes.setup: Jamm presents Leslie with a 'little parting gift'
jokes.punchline: It is a photo of himself and Leslie's face on Yoko Ono's body — and Jamm treats it as a sincere compliment
jokes.explanation: The specific choice of Yoko Ono adds an interesting dimension — culturally loaded choice. 'Horrifying' from Leslie followed by Jamm explaining it as a body compliment is character-perfect cringe. Jamm's sincerity makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: I can't believe I became mayor.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I know. It's unbelievable.

jokes.text: Jamm's farewell karate performance — 'Huh-ho! Oh! Huh! Hai! Huh! He-e-e-e-y! Arigato. Arigato. Arigato. Daytona Beach.'
jokes.setup: Jamm has said his goodbye; the moment seems to be wrapping up
jokes.punchline: Jamm performs an unsolicited karate demonstration, complete with sound effects, and then says 'Daytona Beach' as a farewell
jokes.explanation: 'Daytona Beach' as a farewell word — with zero explanation — is the best part of this bit. The karate is physical gag comedy; 'Daytona Beach' is pure absurdism. Together they're a satisfying Jamm farewell.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: How are your kids so awesome?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well, they have good genes. Their father and I—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I'm not buying that. You must have adopted them.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: April, I gave birth to them. Twice.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's what you're going with?

jokes.text: Maintenance is closed on Fridays — Tom: 'What would our last ride be without one more bureaucratic snafu?'
jokes.setup: The team has finally gotten to maintenance to fix the swing
jokes.punchline: Maintenance is closed on Fridays — another layer of Pawnee bureaucratic incompetence
jokes.explanation: A reliable Parks gag — Pawnee government being inexplicably bad at government. Tom's meta-acknowledgment makes it self-aware. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you are a beautiful, talented, brilliant, powerful musk ox.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You are 40% water, just like the ocean.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Your hair smells like a cinnamon-scented candle.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You are a champion at the sport of life.

jokes.text: Tom's boardroom pitch meeting: 'Accounting nerd.' / 'I'm a congressman, Tom. Can you at least call me Ben?' / 'No can do, accounting nerd. We all knew you before you were a big shot.'
jokes.setup: Tom convenes his 'senior advisory board' to advise on the restaurant expansion
jokes.punchline: Tom refuses to call Ben anything other than 'accounting nerd' despite Ben being a congressman
jokes.explanation: Tom's refusal to update his social hierarchy despite the passage of time and Ben's impressive career is a great character joke. 'We all knew you before you were a big shot' doubles as affectionate and dismissive simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Your baby has a large head.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Smart room!

jokes.text: Ben's calzone advocacy during Tom's restaurant expansion meeting: 'Side note — I would again strongly recommend adding calzones to the menu. Hey, all my data suggests that the country is definitely trending calzone.'
jokes.setup: The board is giving serious business advice about restaurant expansion
jokes.punchline: Ben uses 'all my data' to advocate for calzones — his obsessive calzone love applied to business analytics
jokes.explanation: A perfect Ben callback. The 'again' implies this is not the first time he's pushed calzones in a formal setting. 'All my data suggests the country is definitely trending calzone' — applying congressional/wonk credibility to a pizza preference — is excellent character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I've accomplished more in the last five years than most people accomplish in a lifetime. I'm a businessman, an entrepreneur, a visionary. I've built an empire from nothing.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Mm-hmm.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And you know what the secret is? Dedication. Focus. And a willingness to take risks that other men are too afraid to take.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I stopped listening after you called yourself 'the Sultan of Treats.'

jokes.text: The fake-out: narrator announces Tom lost everything, is 'broke, destitute, and worst of all, swaggerless'
jokes.setup: After Tom's triumphant announcement of 20 Tom's Bistros across America, cut to: narrator revealing he lost everything
jokes.punchline: 'Broke, destitute, and worst of all, swaggerless.' — swagger being the most important loss
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure — the triumphant 'Look out, world, Tommy's about to blow up' cut immediately to ruin. 'And blow up he did. But not in a good way.' is a perfect narration joke. 'Worst of all, swaggerless' is the standout line — the show's values applied to Tom perfectly, where swagger is a more grievous loss than money.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, I've completed your personality quiz. According to the results, I'm 40% you and 60% Donna.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, how did you get me? That's impossible.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Apparently we're more alike than I thought.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: And I'm also a Don? That's redundant.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's not how this works!

jokes.text: Tom watching a documentary about his own failures — that he made himself
jokes.setup: Lucy finds Tom watching something on TV about his failures and tells him to stop
jokes.punchline: 'It's a whole documentary about my failures.' / 'That you made!'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Tom, in his lowest moment, not only made a documentary about his own failures but watches it compulsively. Lucy's 'That you made!' is the perfect exasperated button. This is deeply Tom — his narcissism and media-savviness persisting even through personal disaster. High craft across all dimensions.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm offering all my friends and family a special discount: fifteen percent off.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wow, fifteen percent. That's... that's really generous, Tom. I'm going to go ahead and not buy anything.

jokes.text: 'I lost everything, Lucy — The franchises, most of my money. I had to sell my pocket-square collection. What are people's eyes gonna be drawn to?'
jokes.setup: Tom itemizes his losses
jokes.punchline: His genuine anguish about losing his pocket-square collection — and 'What are people's eyes gonna be drawn to?' as the real tragedy
jokes.explanation: Tom losing 'most of his money' and the pocket squares being listed with equal gravity is perfect Tom comedy. The follow-up question — 'What are people's eyes gonna be drawn to?' — is a genuine existential crisis for this character. Only Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A library named after me? This is the greatest day of my life. I'm going to cry. Happy tears. The best tears.

jokes.text: "Who could have predicted that the country would run out of beef?"
jokes.setup: Lucy is listing factors outside Tom's control that contributed to his failure
jokes.punchline: The country ran out of beef — presented as a plausible market factor with no additional explanation
jokes.explanation: Exceptional absurdist line. Delivered as a matter-of-fact market condition, the idea that 'the country ran out of beef' as a real economic event is delightfully weird. The economy is perfect — one clause, zero explanation. Very quotable and transferable to other contexts. Near-10 for originality.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So which character should I be for the photo?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Be Sergeant Thunderfist, M.D.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Sergeant Thunderfist, M.D.? That's amazing!

jokes.text: Tom's film idea: 'Sniper Race Delta: Beijing Inferno.' — 'I have no idea what it's about, but I have the perfect title.'
jokes.setup: Tom announces his next project: a blockbuster action film
jokes.punchline: He has the perfect title but zero concept for the actual film
jokes.explanation: Tom's approach to entertainment — aesthetics and branding before content — is perfectly captured here. The title itself is a parody of action movie title conventions (four nouns, two proper nouns). The logic of 'title = concept' is pure Tom.

jokes.text: The gift basket from Ben and Leslie to Tom: 'No meat. I checked.' — Ron
jokes.setup: Ron presents a gift basket from Ben and Leslie
jokes.punchline: Ron's first and most important information about the gift: it contains no meat — delivered as a mild disappointment
jokes.explanation: Pure Ron. The first evaluation of any gift — meat content. 'No meat. I checked.' as an aside implying he went through the whole basket looking for meat before delivering it. Perfect economy.

jokes.text: Ron reads the dedication in the gift basket: 'Tom, Here's to your success! Love, Leslie & Ben' — 'Lesile' misspelled
jokes.setup: Ron presents Tom with a gift basket from Ben and Leslie
jokes.punchline: The card reads 'Love, Lesile & Ben' — Leslie misspelled her own name
jokes.explanation: A quiet visual gag for attentive viewers. Leslie — who presumably sent the gift with great care and emotional investment — misspelled her own name. This is a recurring Parks joke about Leslie being simultaneously meticulous and error-prone. Nice for eagle-eyed viewers.

jokes.text: Tom's book talk: running through successful 'types' (Andy, April, Ben, etc.) then 'What do we definitely NOT want to be? A Garry! A Garry! A Garry!'
jokes.setup: Tom is at a book event listing 'types of successful people' from the book
jokes.punchline: The anti-type is Garry — who is in the audience — repeated three times with crowd call-and-response
jokes.explanation: The callback to Garry being perpetually mocked lands particularly well because (1) Tom codified it into a book, (2) Garry is in the audience hearing it, and (3) the crowd chants along. 'He's talking about me.' / 'Hey!' from Garry is the sweet button. Dark but earned by the series.

jokes.text: Tom's book inscription to the group: 'When I think of success, I think of you. You are a true inspiration to me. I love you. Tom Haverford.' / 'Oh, sorry. That's actually for Kendrick Lamar. Here's yours. "Best wishes."' / 'And I mean every word of it.'
jokes.setup: Tom reads a heartfelt, effusive inscription from his book to the group
jokes.punchline: It was meant for Kendrick Lamar — the group gets 'Best wishes.' with the same claimed sincerity
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's best jokes. Perfect misdirection structure: the heartfelt speech builds beautifully to the reveal that it was Kendrick Lamar's inscription. Then 'Best wishes. And I mean every word of it.' turns the deflation into a second punch. The Kendrick Lamar choice specifically (not a generic celebrity) is the right level of unexpected. Tom's straight face makes it. This is excellent joke architecture.

jokes.text: Tom calling the most powerful man in Pawnee to open a maintenance room — it's Mayor Garry
jokes.setup: Tom says they need the help of 'the most powerful man in Pawnee' to open the maintenance room
jokes.punchline: Tom calls Garry — Mayor Gergich — the most powerful man in Pawnee, which is simultaneously accurate and an indignity for Garry
jokes.explanation: A good irony joke — Garry being the 'most powerful man in Pawnee' is true (he's mayor) but the task he's being used for is opening a maintenance room. The mundanity of the request against his title is the joke.

jokes.text: Perd Hapley interviewing Garry after his shock election win — Garry's response: 'Oh, geez. You know what? I have no idea, Perd.'
jokes.setup: Garry wins election in a massive write-in campaign
jokes.punchline: His first statement as mayor-elect: total uncertainty, extreme sincerity, and 'geez'
jokes.explanation: Garry's absolute authenticity in political victory — 'Oh, geez' — is a great character moment. The total absence of spin or preparation in his first statement as mayor-elect is both funny and sweet.

jokes.text: Brandi Maxxx presiding over Garry's swearing-in as 'president of City Council' — introduced as 'star of more than 11,000 adult films in the last two years'
jokes.setup: Garry's official mayoral swearing-in ceremony
jokes.punchline: The presiding official is Brandi Maxxx — a recurring adult film actress character — and her official title is read with full solemnity
jokes.explanation: '11,000 adult films in the last two years' is the specific funny detail — the volume is absurd, the timeframe makes it more so. The solemnity of the swearing-in setting against Brandi's background is well-executed Pawnee comedy.

jokes.text: Garry sworn in for 'the fourth time' — then later 'the tenth time'
jokes.setup: Garry is being sworn in as mayor
jokes.punchline: The ceremony notes it is 'for the fourth time' — then a future flash-forward shows it is now 'for the tenth time'
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Garry's mayoral terms is a satisfying long-form joke — the most put-upon character becoming the most beloved and electorally successful politician in Pawnee. The tenth time is funnier than the fourth.

jokes.text: Garry dies at 100 holding his wife's hand — and they spelled his name wrong on the tombstone: 'Man, Gayle looks amazing.' / 'Yeah, I know.'
jokes.setup: A touching, perfect death — Mayor Garry Gergich dies at 100 surrounded by family
jokes.punchline: Two jokes: (1) they spelled his name wrong on the tombstone / 'Close enough. Hm.' and (2) the first observation is that Gayle looks amazing at 100
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's — and possibly the series' — greatest jokes. The wrong name on the tombstone is the perfect payoff to the entire Jerry/Garry/Larry running gag: even in death, they can't get it right, and 'Close enough. Hm.' suggests it has always been close enough. The second beat — 'Man, Gayle looks amazing' as the FIRST reaction to Garry's peaceful passing — is excellent dark comedy. Both jokes land in the same moment. Exceptional craft.

jokes.text: The Indiana Notary Society's highest honor: 'The 21-Stamp Salute'
jokes.setup: Garry's funeral is described; he receives a special honor
jokes.punchline: The 21-Stamp Salute — a notary version of a 21-gun salute, with stamps
jokes.explanation: Brilliant wordplay/concept. A 21-Stamp Salute is a perfect parody of the 21-Gun Salute, scaled to the tiny gravity of notary work. The word 'salute' applied to stamps is funny before you even process it. One of the episode's most creative comedic inventions.

jokes.text: "'Still Swinging: Parks Gang Reunites for One Last Bang.' That's a little dirty." / "Well, it's a headline, Shauna. Sex sells."
jokes.setup: Shauna the reporter proposes a headline for the swing-fixing story
jokes.punchline: The headline is accidentally sexual; Leslie defends it as smart journalism
jokes.explanation: A modest wordplay joke. The accidental double-entendre in the headline is decent, and Leslie's 'Sex sells' response is character-appropriate (Leslie defending public service journalism). Not exceptional.

jokes.text: Shauna's romantic history summary: 'I had met a guy online, and we started chatting a lot, and I really liked him, but he turned out to be a computer program that a scientist invented to test the gullibility of human women.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks about Shauna's personal life
jokes.punchline: Shauna's latest relationship was with an AI designed specifically to test if women are gullible — a very specific purpose for a scientific program
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the AI's purpose — 'to test the gullibility of human women' — is the funniest element. This is not a catfish or a spam bot; it is a scientific instrument targeted at a specific demographic. The future-episode world-building adds to the absurdism. Leslie's response ('Shauna, you're a very nice person...') is the sweet button.

jokes.text: Woman abandoned at the altar explains: 'He texted me, "game running into overtime. I'll try and stop by."'
jokes.setup: A woman in a wedding dress is alone in the park, looking sad
jokes.punchline: Her fiancé texted that the game ran long — the most dismissive possible abandonment of a wedding
jokes.explanation: 'I'll try and stop by' as a wedding text — the casual language of missing a party applied to abandoning a spouse at the altar — is perfectly deadpan awful. Cringe-funny. The 'try' is the key word.

jokes.text: Tom comforting the sad woman with gum — 'You know what helps me when I'm sad? And I think it might just help you, too. / Gum. My company makes it.'
jokes.setup: Tom sees a crying woman in a wedding dress; he builds up to a sincere piece of wisdom
jokes.punchline: The wisdom is: gum. And Tom's company makes it.
jokes.explanation: Excellent setup/punchline. The extended build-up ('You know what helps me when I'm sad? And I think it might just help you, too.') creates expectation for something profound. The deflation to gum is perfectly timed. The addition of 'My company makes it' adds a self-promotion layer that is pure Tom — sincerity and commerce inseparably fused. High quotability.

jokes.text: Tom and the abandoned woman's wedding — they met five hours ago and are getting married because he gave her gum
jokes.setup: Tom comforted the woman with gum and struck up a conversation
jokes.punchline: Five hours later, Shauna is officiating their wedding — the gum worked too well
jokes.explanation: A satisfying escalation from the gum joke. The vows themselves ('Remember how you offered me gum when I was sad? Yes! I totally remember that.') are the funniest part — the entire romantic foundation is gum. Shauna officiating is a nice bonus (she finally has a happy romantic story to tell, even if it's someone else's).

jokes.text: 'You got to throw your thing.' — Tom throwing his boutonniere like a bouquet after the wedding
jokes.setup: Tom and the woman have just gotten married
jokes.punchline: Someone reminds Tom to throw 'his thing' — he improvises by tossing his boutonniere like a bouquet
jokes.explanation: A nice visual beat. Tom's quick adaptation — treating a boutonniere like a bouquet — is a small physical comedy moment. Decent.

jokes.text: "Not bad craftsmanship, Ron." / "It is perfect craftsmanship."
jokes.setup: Ron has fixed the swing; Leslie compliments him
jokes.punchline: Ron corrects 'not bad' to 'perfect' with total sincerity and zero modesty
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — four words are the punchline. Ron's self-assessment is total, immediate, and unironic. The upgrade from Leslie's gracious 'not bad' to Ron's flat 'perfect' is a great character beat. Could only be Ron.

jokes.text: "I calculate the cost of my labor at $38. I can send the bill to you?"
jokes.setup: The swing has been fixed; everyone is celebrating
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately calculates and presents a bill for his labor to the citizen who asked for the swing repair
jokes.explanation: Perfect Ron joke. The man who just did something genuinely generous (fixing a swing for a stranger) immediately invoices for his labor. Ron's libertarian anti-charity ethos persists even in an act of kindness. The '$38' specificity and the question mark on 'I can send the bill to you?' add to it.

jokes.text: "Don't get emotional, Vaughn. You're embarrassing yourself."
jokes.setup: A board member (Vaughn) appears to be getting emotional at Ron's surprise resignation
jokes.punchline: Ron, who just casually quit his job without explanation, chides someone else for emotional display
jokes.explanation: Excellent button to the resignation joke. Ron created the emotional situation (surprise resignation) and then chides the person reacting emotionally. The hypocrisy is perfect and in-character. 'You're embarrassing yourself' is a great Ron line — transferable and quotable.

jokes.text: Ron's brother immediately volunteers to replace him as chairman: 'I'll do it. Anything else?' / 'Again, Lon, not how corporate governance works.'
jokes.setup: The board is processing Ron's resignation and discussing how to proceed
jokes.punchline: Ron's brother Lon immediately volunteers as if it's a simple substitution, implying this has happened before ('Again, Lon...')
jokes.explanation: 'Again, Lon' implies this has happened before — Lon has tried to assume Ron's corporate positions before. A nice additional beat on the Ron resignation joke.

jokes.text: Ron visiting Ben in Washington: 'This city reeks of swampland and government overreach.' / 'Great to see you as always.'
jokes.setup: Ron arrives at Ben's Washington D.C. home
jokes.punchline: Ron's greeting for the city is a libertarian double-insult; Ben's 'Great to see you as always' accepts this as normal
jokes.explanation: A reliable Ron political philosophy joke. The double-use of 'swampland' (literal and political) is good. Ben's breezy acceptance of Ron's rudeness as normal is the right reaction.

jokes.text: Ron invested his gold and portfolio in... the Lagavulin Distillery (51% ownership): 'You now own 51% of the Lagavulin Distillery.'
jokes.setup: Ben asked what Ron invested in — 'mutual funds? Bonds?'
jokes.punchline: Ron bought controlling interest in his favorite whisky distillery
jokes.explanation: A perfect long-game callback. Ron being told to diversify investments, and his version of diversification being to buy the whisky distillery he loves, is exactly right. Ben's guidance — he invested wisely — paying off in Lagavulin is simultaneously terrible and ideal financial advice for this character. 'Slàinte' as the button is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Ron trying to admit he needs Leslie's help: '...And there are not many people -- I mean, we were workplace proximity acquaintances for many years.' / Leslie: 'Say no more, you big softie.'
jokes.setup: Ron has come to Leslie for personal guidance — a vulnerable admission for him
jokes.punchline: He can't say he needs her help or that she's his friend, landing on 'workplace proximity acquaintances' as the most clinical possible description of their deep bond
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's — and the series' — greatest character jokes. 'Workplace proximity acquaintances' is Ron's maximum emotional reach toward calling Leslie his friend. After seven seasons of their complicated but genuine friendship, this is both deeply funny and deeply moving. It would be painful if Leslie didn't immediately see through it ('Say no more, you big softie'). Maximum character integration — this could only be Ron, to Leslie, in this moment. Exceptional.

jokes.text: Ron: 'You want to stay for dinner? We're having steak.' / '...But we're also hosting several members of the House Subcommittee on Foreign Affairs.' / 'I'll take that steak to go, please, and thank you.'
jokes.setup: Leslie invites Ron to stay for dinner
jokes.punchline: Ron is delighted by steak and immediately deflates when he learns it involves politicians — takes the steak to go
jokes.explanation: Ron's priorities in two sentences: steak yes, politicians no. 'I'll take that steak to go, please, and thank you.' is delivered with complete dignity and certainty. The 'please and thank you' is a Ron formality that makes it funnier. One of his better jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Ron is offered dinner with the House Subcommittee on Foreign Affairs / 'I'll take that steak to go, please and thank you.'
jokes.setup: Ben invites Ron to stay for dinner, noting it also includes members of a congressional subcommittee
jokes.punchline: Ron instantly changes from staying to taking the steak to go upon learning there will be government officials
jokes.explanation: Ron's love of food (especially steak) versus his hatred of government perfectly compressed: he will literally take the steak to go rather than eat it in proximity to Congressional subcommittee members. 'Please and thank you' adds a polite formality that makes the rudeness funnier. High character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Leslie forging Ron's signature: 'I already accepted for you. I still remember how to forge your signature.'
jokes.setup: Leslie offers Ron the Pawnee National Park superintendent job and tells him when to start
jokes.punchline: She already accepted on his behalf and knows how to forge his signature
jokes.explanation: Leslie's willingness to engage in light forgery for the greater good of placing people in the right jobs is very Leslie. 'I still remember how to forge your signature' implies this is not the first time. Warm and funny.

jokes.text: Ron's speech to park rangers ends with: '...we will get along just fine... Though hopefully not too fine, as I'm not looking for any new friends. End of speech.'
jokes.setup: Ron is introducing himself to his new park ranger staff
jokes.punchline: He preemptively caps the potential friendship with his staff before it starts, and formally announces 'End of speech.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ron speech closer. The 'we will get along just fine... Though hopefully not too fine' is a masterful caveat — he literally warns against getting along too well. 'End of speech.' as a literal declaration of having finished is perfect deadpan. High quotability because 'I'm not looking for any new friends' + 'End of speech' is a genuinely usable phrase.

jokes.text: "Damn, that food was good! I've said it before, and I'll say it again — Joe Biden knows his way around the seafood risotto."
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are at dinner at what we realize is the Biden White House
jokes.punchline: Leslie has said this before — Joe Biden's seafood risotto cooking ability is a known established fact in her world
jokes.explanation: The implication that Leslie has dined with the Bidens multiple times and makes a specific point of noting Joe's seafood risotto skill is wonderfully absurd. 'You've said that before?' from Ben — the 'I've said it before' implying this is a recurring Leslie testimonial — is the button. The choice of risotto specifically (a laborious dish) adds to it.

jokes.text: "Someone's been reading my kindergarten dream journal." — Leslie on being asked about running for governor
jokes.setup: A DNC contact mentions Leslie as a gubernatorial candidate
