jokes.punchline: Leslie has a kindergarten dream journal and 'governor of Indiana' is in it — the revelation that this has been a lifelong ambition documented in a children's journal
jokes.explanation: A perfect Leslie line. The kindergarten dream journal exists and contains gubernatorial ambitions. The casual delivery ('Someone's been reading my kindergarten dream journal') implies she has multiple such journals and this is unremarkable. Very high character integration. Extremely quotable and transferable.

jokes.text: Ben is also approached about running for governor — the awkward simultaneous disclosure between Ben and Leslie
jokes.setup: Leslie is excited about the governor approach; she tells Ben
jokes.punchline: Ben reveals Jen also approached him — both were simultaneously pitched on the same governorship by different operatives
jokes.explanation: The awkward 'Oh.' / 'Oh!' / '...Right. Yeah. No, no. I mean, obviously...' back-and-forth is good cringe comedy for a couple navigating a delicate situation. The 'Obviously' repeated with increasing hollowness is the key joke.

jokes.text: Ben and Leslie's governor conversation: both pro/con lists are identical; 'The only con of you running would be that I don't get to run, and vice versa.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie try to logically work out who should run for governor
jokes.punchline: Every pro for Leslie is also a pro for Ben — the lists are identical — leaving them at an impasse that can only be resolved by coin flip
jokes.explanation: A clever structural joke about how well-matched Ben and Leslie are. The parity of their qualifications creates a recursive logical trap. Functional and character-appropriate but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Leslie wanting the coin to 'eventually make its way into the Smithsonian'
jokes.setup: Leslie proposes flipping a coin to decide who runs for governor
jokes.punchline: She already has a post-flip plan for the coin: the Smithsonian
jokes.explanation: Pure Leslie. Even in a moment of deliberately leaving things to chance, she's already planning the historical preservation of the coin. The Smithsonian detail is the right level of grandiose for her self-regard.

jokes.text: Ben and Leslie's teenage kids blowing them off at dinner: 'Hey, I'm gonna eat in my room because I have to study.' / 'Can we go to Bobby's house and watch the game? Did you finish your homework? Yes. Okay. Don't forget to-- / Be back by 8:00. Bye, Dad. Bye, Mom.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben excitedly call the kids for dinner, clearly wanting a family moment
jokes.punchline: The kids scatter in all directions without ceremony — Leslie's 'Get your ice skates!' follows them out
jokes.explanation: A good observational moment — the contrast between Leslie's intensity around togetherness and her kids' total indifference to it. The callback structure of Leslie's episode-long desire to have everyone in the same place being undercut by her own children is a nice irony.

jokes.text: Ann and Leslie catching up on hair growth pills: 'That's from the pills I was telling you about. / I took some of those, but I don't know. They didn't do anything, and they kind of upset my stomach. / No, no, no. You're supposed to crack them and leave them on your hair overnight, not eat them. / Oh, no. / Well, it's confusing 'cause they're delicious.'
jokes.setup: Ann's hair is amazing; Leslie comments that she tried the pills
jokes.punchline: Leslie was eating hair growth pills because they're 'delicious' — she didn't read the instructions
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The revelation builds through three steps: Ann's great hair → Leslie tried the pills → Leslie was EATING them → 'they're delicious.' The last beat — finding hair-application pills delicious — is the right amount of absurd. Leslie's total lack of self-consciousness about this is perfect.

jokes.text: Donna revealing a massive diamond watch under duct tape on her wrist: 'What's with all the duct tape?' / 'Just because I work for the federal government doesn't mean I have to advertise it to everyone.'
jokes.setup: Donna works for a nonprofit/foundation now; someone notices duct tape on her wrist
jokes.punchline: Under the duct tape is a massive diamond watch — Donna hiding her wealth because she now works in the nonprofit sector
jokes.explanation: A great visual/character joke. Donna's solution to the perceived conflict between nonprofit work and personal luxury is duct tape. The reveal (diamonds under tape) is the visual punchline. 'I do that literally 50 times a day' adds a behavioral bonus. High character integration — only Donna.

jokes.text: Ron's reaction to Garry being mayor: 'Yes. Neither can anyone else.'
jokes.setup: Garry says 'I just still can't believe it' about being mayor
jokes.punchline: Ron agrees — no one can believe it — but frames it as disbelief rather than shared wonder
jokes.explanation: Economy of the Ron-mocking-Garry joke. Garry's self-wonder and Ron's total agreement — for different reasons — in five words. Perfect.

jokes.text: April to Ann about her kids: 'Your kids are, like, surprisingly awesome. / Did you use an egg donor or give Chris a hall pass for a night?'
jokes.setup: April compliments Ann's children
jokes.punchline: The compliment is immediately followed by April questioning the biological source of children who are 'too good' to be Chris and Ann's
jokes.explanation: Classic April — a compliment that contains an insult. 'Hall pass for a night' is memorably blunt. Ann's 'Once again, they are my biological children. Once again, I don't believe you.' dynamic is a running exchange that works.

jokes.text: Andy confuses Chris for 'Chip Traeger': 'Well, there he is. Chip Traeger, you old son of a gun.' / 'Andy, it's Chris.' / 'Is it? Huh.'
jokes.setup: Andy reunites with Chris at the party
jokes.punchline: Andy greets Chris by a completely wrong name with total confidence; when corrected, he's only mildly interested in the information
jokes.explanation: 'Is it? Huh.' as Andy's response to being corrected is very good. He doesn't apologize or seem embarrassed — he processes the correction with mild curiosity. Classic Andy earnestness about his own obliviousness.

jokes.text: Leslie's Ann compliments escalating: 'Ann, you rainbow-infused space unicorn... Ann, you beautiful, sassy mannequin-come-to-life... Ann, you opalescent tree shark.'
jokes.setup: Leslie sees Ann for the first time in a while
jokes.punchline: Leslie deploys the famous absurd Ann compliments — 'rainbow-infused space unicorn,' 'opalescent tree shark' — with the third being the most nonsensical
jokes.explanation: A series-beloved running gag delivered one final time with appropriate escalation. 'Opalescent tree shark' is a new entry and it's a beauty — two completely incompatible nouns joined by an unusual adjective. High impact because audiences who know the show react to this running gag with enormous affection. The meta-comment ('Leslie, you are the master of the metaphor') acknowledges the gag.

jokes.text: Chris's health watch: 'You are extremely healthy. I do that literally 50 times a day.' / 'Aren't you afraid that thing might give you cancer?' / 'Well, I am now.'
jokes.setup: Chris is checking health metrics on his wrist device obsessively
jokes.punchline: Donna asks if he fears cancer from the device; Chris immediately adopts the fear
jokes.explanation: Chris's health anxiety being immediately triggered by an offhand remark is good character comedy. 'Well, I am now.' is a great quick reaction beat. Character-specific to Chris.

jokes.text: Ron examining baby Jack: 'Doctor said he has a remarkably large head. Just like his old man.' / 'Yeah, we know what that means — More smart room for it.'
jokes.setup: Ron examines baby Jack and notes the large head
jokes.punchline: Andy's explanation for the large head: 'More smart room for it' — Andy's version of the 'big head = smart' folk wisdom
jokes.explanation: 'More smart room for it' is a genuinely funny Andy-ism — his confident folk explanation using half-formed logic. Ron's dignified 'Strong handshake. Well done, you two.' to a newborn is also a nice beat.

jokes.text: Ben explaining Cones of Dunshire to someone at the party: 'Oh, it's a common misconception that the Oculus holds all of the power. It's actually the Lamplighter.'
jokes.setup: Party scene; Ben is explaining his board game to someone
jokes.punchline: Ben in his element — correcting a Cones of Dunshire misconception with total seriousness
jokes.explanation: A nice callback that confirms the Lamplighter/Oculus mythology of Cones of Dunshire is sufficiently developed that people have misconceptions about it. Ben's passion for correcting these is character-perfect.

jokes.text: Tom's talking head to the camera — addressing the camera itself: 'I know you probably imagined us meeting once a year for a rendezvous, but I'm happy... I guess what I'm saying is, I'm out of your league, and you need to move on.'
jokes.setup: Tom gives what appears to be a talking-head confessional — but the 'you' seems to be the camera/show itself
jokes.punchline: Tom is breaking up with the documentary crew / the show — telling the camera it needs to move on from him
jokes.explanation: A meta-joke where Tom is apparently breaking up with the documentary camera, framing the end of the show through Tom's narcissism. 'I'm out of your league, and you need to move on' is a genuinely funny way for a character to acknowledge a series finale. High originality for this episode.

jokes.text: Tom to Ann — completely out of earshot of Donna — telling her he's 'out of her league' and she needs to move on, while she stopped listening when he called her 'sugarpea'
jokes.setup: Tom sidles up to Ann apparently to deliver a heartfelt message about their old relationship
jokes.punchline: 'I stopped listening when you called me sugarpea.' — Ann's complete disengagement and Tom's oblivious continued speech
jokes.explanation: Tom telling Ann she needs to 'move on' from him while he is clearly still invested is classic character comedy. Ann tuning out immediately at 'sugarpea' is the right response. The joke is about Tom's continued delusion balanced against Ann's complete indifference.

jokes.text: 'Ann! Oh, my God. It's happening. It's totally happening. Our kids are falling in love. This is good. Remember, if this is ever gonna work, we have to pretend to disapprove.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann notice their kids interacting
jokes.punchline: Leslie has a strategy prepared — pretend to disapprove to make it more attractive — and then immediately blows it
jokes.explanation: Leslie's inability to contain her enthusiasm for her own plans is a well-worn but well-executed character joke here. The immediate failure ('Leslie, no.') is a good quick beat.

jokes.text: Ann: 'Ann Arbor, Michigan, is literally the greatest city that I've ever lived in. But Pawnee is better. So we're moving back.'
jokes.setup: Ann is talking about her life in Ann Arbor
jokes.punchline: Ann acknowledges Ann Arbor is great but concludes Pawnee — a city the show has repeatedly established as objectively terrible — is better
jokes.explanation: Works as a warm joke about Pawnee's unlikely appeal. The show's long-running joke about Pawnee being a terrible city being undercut by everyone's love for it is touched on here.

jokes.text: Tom's book quiz: 'I took the quiz in your book about what kind of person I am. I'm a Ron.' / 'Ha. I'm usually a Tom, but sometimes, I'm a Don.' / 'Last time I took it, I was a Tom.' / 'What? No! No! No! Take it again! I got to go recalibrate the quiz.'
jokes.setup: Ron tells Tom he took the quiz in Tom's book
jokes.punchline: Ron got 'Ron' — disappointing no one. But then Ron reveals he got 'Tom' previously, which sends Tom into a spiral about his quiz's validity.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. Tom's quiz getting 'Ron' for Ron is expected. But Ron revealing he previously scored 'Tom' — and Tom's complete meltdown about quiz validity — is the real joke. 'I got to go recalibrate the quiz' is the perfect line, implying Tom would rather break the quiz than accept that Ron registered as a Tom. The 'sometimes I'm a Don' from Tom is a funny extra beat.

jokes.text: Tom's book quiz: 'I took the quiz in your book about what kind of person I am. I'm a Ron.' / 'Ha. I'm usually a Tom, but sometimes I'm a Don.' / 'What? No! No! No! Take it again! I got to go recalibrate the quiz.'
jokes.setup: Ron informs Tom he tested as a 'Ron' in Tom's own personality quiz
jokes.punchline: Tom's complete inability to accept this result — 'Take it again! I got to go recalibrate the quiz' — and Ron's casual 'I'm sometimes a Don'
jokes.explanation: The idea that Ron Swanson — the anti-Tom — has tested as a Tom is perfectly absurd and destabilizing for Tom. His response ('No! No! I've got to go recalibrate the quiz') is wonderful — he's more concerned with quiz accuracy than Ron's actual personality. The 'sometimes a Don' from Ron is an additional great beat.

jokes.text: Leslie's toast: 'First of all, I just have to say that all of you in the same room at the same time with your children here, it's like... It's the greatest thing that's ever happened in the history of America.'
jokes.setup: Leslie prepares to toast the group
jokes.punchline: Describing a group of friends in a living room as 'the greatest thing that's ever happened in the history of America' — Leslie's total lack of proportionality
jokes.explanation: Solid Leslie hyperbole — a well-worn character note but delivered with genuine warmth that makes it sweet and funny simultaneously.

jokes.text: Tom's 'friends and family' deal at his restaurant: '3% off.'
jokes.setup: Tom invites everyone to celebrate at Tom's Bistro under 'original management' with the friends-and-family deal
jokes.punchline: The friends-and-family discount is 3% — a number so small as to be insulting
jokes.explanation: Perfect Tom joke. The build-up ('you all get the friends-and-family deal') creates expectation for generosity, and '3% off' is the perfect deflation — technically a discount, practically insulting. Leslie's 'Oh my God. You're too generous, Tom.' response is the ideal button.

jokes.text: Ron corrects the citizen's characterization of the swing-fixing team as 'public servants': 'Actually, none of these people works in local government. This is a group of private citizens and one misguided federal employee meddling where she does not belong.'
jokes.setup: Leslie wraps up the swing-fixing with 'Local government at its very best.'
jokes.punchline: Ron pedantically corrects this on ideological grounds — they are NOT government, they are private citizens, and Leslie is a misguided federal employee
jokes.explanation: An excellent series-finale joke. Ron's libertarian anti-government philosophy gets its final statement — even in a warm moment of civic goodness, he must correct the ideological framing. 'One misguided federal employee meddling where she does not belong' for Leslie is particularly good. The show's central tension (Ron hates government / Leslie loves it) resolved with a Ron win. 'For once, could you just-- No.' from Leslie is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Donna: 'Ah. The lighting's all wrong. I'm gonna send you a glamour shot. Just Photoshop me in later.'
jokes.setup: Everyone gathers for a final group photo
jokes.punchline: Donna opts out of the photo to be Photoshopped in later with a better shot — treating a casual farewell photo like a professional shoot
jokes.explanation: Peak Donna. Her commitment to looking fabulous extending even to a casual friends photo, and her solution (Photoshop later) being completely reasonable to her, is very in-character. The lighting note shows she's already assessed the shot.

jokes.text: April: 'I'm not gonna show up in that picture anyway because I'm a vampire.'
jokes.setup: The group is gathering for a photo
jokes.punchline: April's excuse for not joining is that she's a vampire and won't appear in photos
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy and character integration. April's gothic persona extended to claiming vampire status to explain photo non-appearance. The deadpan certainty is total. High quotability.

jokes.text: Andy's character choice dilemma: 'Hey, babe, for this picture, should I be Burt Macklin, Johnny Karate, or my new character, Sergeant Thunderfist, M.D.?' / 'Where did you get that?' / 'Found it in a sandbox.' / 'Ew!'
jokes.setup: Andy is deciding how to pose for the group photo
jokes.punchline: He has a new character: Sergeant Thunderfist, M.D. — and he is holding a prop he found in a sandbox
jokes.explanation: The joke has two layers: 'Sergeant Thunderfist, M.D.' as a new Andy character (the M.D. adds absurd medical credentials to an action name) and the sandbox prop that nobody asks more about. 'Go Macklin. Macklin's the hottest.' from April is a sweet button.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Get on with it. I can't hold this smile forever. I look ridiculous.'
jokes.setup: The group is slowly assembling for the photo; Ron is in position
jokes.punchline: Ron has been smiling — an enormous effort for him — and is running out of capacity for it
jokes.explanation: A perfect series-finale moment from Ron. His smiling is itself the vulnerability — he IS happy to be here, and 'I look ridiculous' is his embarrassed acknowledgment. The line works because we know what it means for Ron to smile. High character integration and a genuinely moving-funny beat for the finale.

tmdb_overview: The Parks gang completes one last task together, before saying goodbye to Pawnee.
insight: Seventy jokes in 58 minutes—character-driven absurdism sustains a solid, if unspectacular finale.
